title: Types and Shadows
lead: Typology reads people, events and institutions as patterns (types) that later events repeat and fulfill. The Hebrew Bible already does this, as when the prophets describe a new exodus. The New Testament reads such patterns as pointing to Christ (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 10:6, 11; Hebrews 8:5). Jewish tradition has its own principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, and its own objections to the Christian method.

sections.b: Before the New Testament, Israel's own writers read new events through old ones. Isaiah describes the return from Babylon as a new exodus, with a way through the sea and water in the desert (Isaiah 43:16–19; 51:9–11). Joshua is a new Moses: he parts the Jordan and is told to take off his sandals on holy ground (Joshua 3:7; 5:15; compare Exodus 3:5). Elijah travels forty days to Horeb, the mountain of Moses, and hears God there (1 Kings 19:8–18). Michael Fishbane's study of such "inner-biblical" interpretation showed how widely the Bible reads itself this way. Jews, Christians and critical scholars all recognize these patterns.
sections.refs: Isaiah 43:16–19; Isaiah 51:9–11; Joshua 3:7; Joshua 5:15; Exodus 3:5; 1 Kings 19:8–18

sections.h: Typology in the New Testament and the church
sections.b: Paul calls Adam "a type of the one who was to come" (Romans 5:14). He says Israel's wilderness experiences were typoi, "examples," for the church (1 Corinthians 10:6) and that they happened typikōs, "as examples" (10:11). Hebrews calls the tabernacle "a copy" (antitypa) of the true sanctuary (Hebrews 9:24) and the law "a shadow of the good things to come" (Hebrews 10:1), and 1 Peter 3:21 calls baptism the antitype of the flood. Jesus compares himself to Jonah (Matthew 12:40) and to the bronze serpent (John 3:14). The church fathers extended the method widely: Joseph, Isaac, Moses, David and many others became types of Christ. Most interpreters distinguish typology, which links real events by a shared pattern, from allegory, which finds hidden meanings in details.
sections.refs: Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 10:6–11; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:24; Hebrews 10:1; 1 Peter 3:21; Matthew 12:40; John 3:14

sections.h: Jewish typology: "the deeds of the fathers"
sections.b: Ramban (Nachmanides) states the Jewish principle in his commentary on Genesis 12:6, drawing on Midrash Tanhuma (Lekh Lekha 9): "everything that happened to the fathers is a sign for the children." For him Abraham's going down to Egypt in famine foreshadows Israel's descent and exodus, and Jacob's dealings with Esau foreshadow Israel's history under Rome. The rabbis also taught, "As the first redeemer, so the last redeemer" (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:9): Moses rode on a donkey (Exodus 4:20) and so will the Messiah (Zechariah 9:9); Moses brought down manna, and so will the Messiah. Jewish typology points from Israel's past to Israel's own future.

Jewish readers have long objected that Christian typology can empty Israel's story of its own meaning, as if Joseph or the exodus mattered only as a preview of Christ, and that the method was used in polemic claiming the church had replaced Israel. Many Christian interpreters today grant the point and insist that a type keeps its own history and value. Among scholars, Leonhard Goppelt's Typos (1939) defined typology as a correspondence between real events in salvation history. After the Second World War, Gerhard von Rad argued that typology is a natural way of reading the Old Testament as a story of promise and fulfillment, while Walther Eichrodt warned against using it loosely.
